name: master ragu
instructions:
FOUR VARIANTS UNDER ONE PASTA-RAGU SHAPE. All share: tomato base + a protein (real or faux meat, or lentils) + acid (wine or wine vinegar) + soffrito-style aromatics + pasta. Variant A is the canonical bolognese and gets the headline treatment.

=== VARIANT A — MARCELLA BOLOGNESE (CANONICAL) ===

The load-bearing recipe in this family. Marcella Hazan, Essentials of Classic Italian Cooking. If 'italian ragu' means one thing in this cookbook, it's this one.

INGREDIENTS:
- vegetable oil + butter (the fat)
- yellow onions, celery, carrots — finely diced soffrito
- ground beef (or impossible meat as the substitute)
- milk
- nutmeg
- white wine
- canned tomatoes
- black pepper
- pasta (traditionally tagliatelle, not spaghetti)
- parmesan cheese for serving

TECHNIQUE — MARCELLA'S NON-NEGOTIABLES:
1. Cook the beef ONLY until it loses raw color. Do NOT brown it. Browning gives a different (and lesser) ragu.
2. Milk goes in BEFORE wine. The milk coats the meat and protects it from the wine acid; reversing the order changes the texture.
3. Bare-simmer for THREE+ HOURS uncovered. Splash in water if it dries out. The long uncovered simmer is what makes it a bolognese; cutting time turns it into a generic meat sauce.
4. Fat should separate at the end. That's the visual signal you're done.

=== VARIANT B — EGGPLANT RAGU (VEGAN) ===

- Sauté finely diced yellow onions and shallots in olive oil with garlic.
- Add diced eggplant and portabella mushrooms; cook down until soft and browned.
- Add ground vegan meat, break it up, cook through.
- Stir in canned tomatoes, porcini mushroom powder, nutritional yeast, red wine vinegar. Simmer until thickened.
- Toss with pasta.

=== VARIANT C — MUSHROOM LENTIL RAGU (VEGETARIAN) ===

- Brown mushrooms HARD in olive oil — get real color on them. Set aside.
- Sauté yellow onions in the same pan. Deglaze with red wine; reduce.
- Add lentils, canned tomatoes, and enough water to cover the lentils. Simmer until lentils are tender.
- Return mushrooms to the pan; warm through.
- Finish OFF HEAT with parmesan, nutritional yeast, basil, and parsley. Salt and black pepper to taste.
- Toss with pasta.

=== VARIANT D — FIRE ROASTED MEATBALLS ===

- Shape impossible meat into meatballs and brown in olive oil.
- Add FIRE ROASTED canned tomatoes (not regular — the fire-roasted character is the dish's signature), red wine vinegar, fennel seeds, bay leaf.
- Simmer until thickened.
- Toss with pasta.

=== VARIANT E — NISHA VORA'S LENTIL BOLOGNESE (VEGAN, TOMATO-PASTE-FORWARD) ===

From Nisha Vora / Rainbow Plant Life. Distinct from variant C (mushroom lentil ragu) — this version has NO mushrooms in the base and follows a more traditionally-bolognese technique (tomato paste caramelized in the fond, red wine deglaze, long simmer, balsamic finish). Red lentils + finely chopped walnuts do the meat-analog work; the tomato paste + crushed tomatoes carry the umami. ~55 min total, much faster than the 3-hour bolognese in variant A.

INGREDIENTS (serves 6):
- 1 1/2 tbsp olive oil
- 1 large onion, diced
- 4 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 tsp dried oregano
- 1 tsp dried thyme (or more oregano if you don't have thyme)
- 1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
- freshly ground black pepper
- 1 (5.3-oz / 150g) TUBE of tomato paste (see notes — tube is load-bearing, not canned)
- 1/2 cup (120mL) dry red wine (optional but recommended — malbec / chianti / tempranillo / sangiovese / merlot / cabernet sauvignon / pinot noir / syrah)
- 3 cups (720mL) vegetable broth
- 1 cup (185g) RED lentils, soaked 30-60 min first (see notes)
- 1/4 cup (32g) walnuts, crushed finely (see notes on chopping)
- 1 (14.5-oz / 410g) can crushed tomatoes OR whole peeled tomatoes crushed by hand
- 12-16 oz pasta (long-wide preferred: tagliatelle, pappardelle, fettuccine; ridged tube also works: rigatoni, penne rigate; gnocchi works)
- 1 tbsp high-quality aged balsamic vinegar (or 1-2 tsp brown/coconut/cane sugar as a sub)
- flat-leaf parsley or fresh basil, chopped, for garnish

PROCEDURE:
1. Soak the red lentils in cool water for 30-60 min. Meanwhile, prep everything else (chop onion + garlic, finely chop walnuts).
2. Heat 12-inch deep sauté pan or Dutch oven on medium-high. Add olive oil; when shimmering, add onions + pinch of salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until light-brown fond forms on the pan surface (~5 min). Deglaze with a few spoons of water and stir. Continue cooking, adding more water every few minutes and stirring frequently to prevent burning, until onions are softened and golden brown (9-10 min total).
3. Add garlic, thyme, oregano, 1 1/2 tsp salt, and pepper. Stir frequently, cook 60-90 sec.
4. Stir in the ENTIRE TUBE OF TOMATO PASTE. Cook 2-3 min, stirring very frequently, until it caramelizes and turns darker red.
5. OPTIONAL — DEGLAZE WITH RED WINE: pour in wine, scrape up browned bits, cook 1-2 min until alcohol smell burns off and mixture is jammy.
6. Pour in vegetable broth to deglaze. Add drained lentils and crushed walnuts; stir. Bring to a boil, reduce to medium-low for a rapid simmer, cook 20 min stirring occasionally.
7. Add the crushed tomatoes. Simmer another 15-20 min (or 20 min for more developed flavor) until lentils are tender but still al dente. Stir occasionally to prevent sticking. If using crushed tomatoes (not whole crushed by hand), may need a little water or lower heat.
8. Meanwhile, cook pasta in generously salted water to just al dente. Reserve a ladle of pasta water. Drain (don't rinse).
9. Taste for seasoning. Finish the bolognese with the balsamic vinegar (or sugar sub) and stir.
10. Add the hot pasta to the bolognese, toss until coated, add pasta water as needed. Garnish with fresh parsley or basil.
notes:
THE RAGU SHAPE — WHAT THESE FOUR HAVE IN COMMON:
1. A tomato base (canned tomatoes in all four; fire-roasted in variant D specifically).
2. A protein: real meat (A), faux meat (B, D), or lentils (C).
3. An acid: white wine (A), red wine vinegar (B, D), or red wine (C). Pick one per variant — don't mix or substitute across variants.
4. Soffrito-style aromatics: yellow onion is always in; celery/carrot/shallots/garlic vary.
5. Served over pasta.

DISTINCTION FROM LENTIL-MUSHROOM-STEW: that dish is a stew, not a ragu — broth-forward, served as a soup, explicitly anti-canned-tomato and anti-tomato-paste, uses stock not pasta. It has overlapping headline ingredients with variant C but contradictory rules. Don't merge the two.

WHY BOLOGNESE GETS THE HEADLINE: variant A is the canonical italian ragu — Marcella Hazan's recipe is the cookbook's reference point. The three non-negotiables (don't brown the beef, milk before wine, three-hour uncovered simmer) define what 'bolognese' means here. Other variants borrow the ragu shape but don't try to be bolognese — they're distinct dishes, not vegetarianized bolognese.

WHY MILK IS IN BOLOGNESE BUT NOT THE OTHERS: milk's role is to coat the beef and tenderize it during the long simmer. The vegan/vegetarian variants don't have raw beef to protect, and the acid stress (red wine vinegar in B and D, red wine in C) is built into the recipe rather than fought against. Adding milk to variants B/C/D doesn't help — it muddies the tomato.

FAUX MEAT SUBSTITUTIONS:
- Variant A (bolognese): impossible meat works as a substitute for ground beef. Don't substitute ground vegan meat for ground beef in bolognese — impossible has the right fat profile, ground vegan meat reads off.
- Variant B (eggplant): ground vegan meat is the canonical choice. Impossible also works but is overkill.
- Variant D (meatballs): impossible meat shaped into meatballs. The shaping matters — the meatball format is the distinguishing texture; without it, this becomes generic vegan ragu.

FIRE ROASTED TOMATOES ARE FOR VARIANT D ONLY: don't reach for fire-roasted in the other variants. Variant A (bolognese) wants regular canned tomatoes — fire-roasted reads too smoky against the milk-and-nutmeg base. Variants B and C also want regular canned. Fire-roasted is the signature of variant D; using it elsewhere is wrong.

NO BASIL OR PARSLEY IN BOLOGNESE OR EGGPLANT: variants A and B don't take fresh herb finishes well. Bolognese's long simmer and milk-and-nutmeg base is its own register; basil/parsley on top reads as an addition that doesn't help. Eggplant ragu is similar — porcini powder and nutritional yeast do the umami work, fresh herbs are a distraction. Variant C (mushroom lentil) DOES want basil and parsley off heat — the lighter wine-and-lentil base is brightened by them.

TAGLIATELLE OVER SPAGHETTI FOR VARIANT A: marcella was explicit that bolognese is for tagliatelle, not spaghetti. The wide flat noodle holds the meat sauce; spaghetti slides under it. Variants B, C, D are more forgiving — penne or other shapes work fine.

=== VARIANT E NOTES — NISHA VORA'S LENTIL BOLOGNESE ===

SOURCE: Nisha Vora, Rainbow Plant Life. 10-ingredient vegan lentil bolognese. ~55 min total (much faster than variant A's 3+ hours).

HOW IT DIFFERS FROM VARIANT C (MUSHROOM LENTIL RAGU): both are vegan lentil-forward, but they're structurally different:
- Variant C uses whole browned mushrooms + red wine + generic lentils + parmesan/nutritional yeast finish. More stew-like, mushroom-forward.
- Variant E uses RED lentils specifically + walnuts (no mushrooms in the base) + a whole tube of tomato paste caramelized + balsamic vinegar finish. Follows classical bolognese technique more closely (paste-caramelize + wine deglaze + long simmer) but does it in an hour instead of three.
Both valid; pick based on whether you want mushroom-forward stew (C) or a more traditionally-bolognese-shaped tomato-paste-forward sauce (E).

TOMATO PASTE FROM A TUBE, NOT A CAN — LOAD-BEARING: Nisha is explicit and I trust her on this — canned tomato paste leaves a tinny metallic flavor here that ruins the sauce. Tube tomato paste (Amore, Cento, Mutti, San Merican; Whole Foods 365 or Trader Joe's for budget) is cooked at lower temp and preserved with salt (canned is preserved with citric acid) — brighter, truer tomato flavor. This isn't a nitpick; use a tube.

RED LENTILS SOAKED FIRST — 30 MIN MINIMUM: soaking softens the lentils and cuts the cook time significantly. Skip and they'll take 45-60 min to soften in the sauce instead of ~20 min. Red split lentils (masoor dal from indian groceries) cook even faster. Brown or green lentils work as a sub but need an extra 5-10 min and give the sauce more bite (less melt-into-sauce).

WALNUTS FINELY CHOPPED — MELT INTO THE SAUCE: crush walnuts in a food processor or spice grinder, or knife-chop very finely. Coarser walnut pieces leave hard bits in the finished sauce (not terrible but not ideal). Fine walnuts add meaty body and blend into the sauce texture.

TOAST THE WALNUTS FIRST (BETH'S TIP, ADOPTED HERE): Nisha suggests toasting walnuts in oven or dry skillet to enhance flavor. Same principle as the lentil-wellington walnut-toasting note — toasted walnut is where the meat-analog umami actually lives.

NUT-FREE SUB: Nisha's options — sauté finely diced mushrooms after the onions, OR add 1/2-1 tsp porcini mushroom powder with the broth. Latter is the cleaner sub since it stays in Nisha's recipe timeline.

BALSAMIC FINISH — QUALITY MATTERS OR SKIP: 1 tbsp high-quality aged balsamic. Nisha is explicit that a cheap balsamic just adds watery sourness and doesn't help. Better to omit than to use cheap balsamic. Sugar sub (1-2 tsp brown/coconut/cane) works if the sauce is too sour without.

RED WINE OPTIONAL — REAL DIFFERENCE THOUGH: 1/2 cup dry red deglaze after the tomato paste caramelizes. Recipe works fine without it, but the wine adds noticeable richness and complements the tomato paste. Any dry red works (see ingredient list for the range).

WANT-TO-TRY (FROM COMMENTS SECTION): reader Julie added grated carrot and fresh tomatoes, said it worked well. Grated carrot in particular is a legitimate soffrito-adjacent addition worth trying — Nisha's original skips the classic mirepoix (celery + carrot), and carrot would push this closer to a traditional soffrito base.

CRITIQUE FROM A COMMENTER: one reviewer (JKL) said the sauce reads too acidic without dairy, felt it needed a milk / dairy component to balance the wine acid. Worth noting if you find the sauce sharp — could try Nisha's balsamic-out / sugar-in path, or (departing from her recipe) add a splash of unsweetened plant milk near the end for a bolognese-adjacent milk protective step.

=== This master is deliberately the protein-forward, long-simmered (or ~1-hour Nisha-style), cutting-board-cut side of the italian-pasta-sauce family. Everything on the OTHER side of these axes belongs in master-italian-tomato-sauce-and-pesto:
- PROTEIN-FREE SAUCES AND PESTI: no meat, no faux meat, no lentils. Nuts and cheese fill the fat-and-protein slot over there; the absence of a real protein slot is the tell.
- FAST (<45 MIN) OR RAW: Hazan's 3-ingredient simmer is 45 min; the halfway-pesto variant B is 30-40 min; the sicilian pesto rosso variant C is raw and blended in a food processor. Ragu's canonical time investment (3+ hour bare simmer for bolognese) doesn't fit there.
- WHOLE-OR-BLENDED, NOT KNIFE-DICED: ragu's soffrito (finely diced onion + celery + carrot in bolognese, diced eggplant + mushrooms in eggplant, hard-browned mushroom pieces in mushroom-lentil, whole meatballs in D) stays visible in the finished dish. Over there, Hazan halves the onion and discards it (no dicing at all), variant B goes into an immersion blender, variant C is a raw food processor pesto. No discrete chunks survive.
- PASTA-FINISHER, NOT MAIN-DISH SAUCE: pesto and tomato sauces there are pasta-finishers — pasta and sauce as equal partners. Ragu is the main event of the plate and the pasta is a delivery vehicle.
The cutting-board vs blender/whole distinction is the biggest one — everything else stacks with it. If you're reaching for a knife to dice a soffrito, you're here; if you're halving an onion to fish out or blending everything smooth, you're over there.
